report:
## Conclusion

You're right — the strongest and most current evidence indicates arthroscopic surgery (lavage, debridement, or partial meniscectomy) does **not** meaningfully help knee osteoarthritis.

**Key evidence:**

1. **Sham-controlled RCTs**: Moseley et al.'s landmark placebo-controlled trial found that patients receiving actual arthroscopic debridement or lavage for knee OA reported no better pain relief or function than those receiving sham surgery (skin incisions only) (NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259). A second RCT by Kirkley et al. confirmed arthroscopic surgery plus optimized medical/physical therapy provided no additional benefit over optimized therapy alone in moderate-to-severe knee OA (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333).

2. **Cochrane systematic reviews**: A Cochrane review concluded arthroscopic debridement probably does not improve pain or function compared to placebo (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD005118_arthroscopic-debridement-osteoarthritis-knee). A more recent 2022 Cochrane review of arthroscopic surgery for degenerative knee disease (including OA and meniscal tears) reached similar conclusions of little to no benefit (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease).

3. **Clinical practice guidelines**: Based on this cumulative evidence, an international expert panel publishing in *The BMJ* (2017) issued a **strong recommendation against** arthroscopic knee surgery for degenerative knee disease, including osteoarthritis and degenerative meniscal tears (https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982/).

**Bottom line:** High-quality, sham-controlled trials and systematic reviews consistently show arthroscopy provides no meaningful benefit over placebo or conservative therapy for knee osteoarthritis, and major guidelines now recommend against it.
